title: Comparing Concurrency Models
summary: Synthesis — how to actually choose between threads, async/await, actors, and CSP for a real system, what each protects you from, and how production systems mix models instead of picking just one.

slides.markdown:
This group opened with one problem — shared mutable state under concurrency — and showed five structurally different responses to it: raw threads, async/await, actors, CSP, and lock-free/STM, plus structured concurrency as an orthogonal lifetime discipline layered on top of any of them.

This closing topic doesn't introduce a new model — it puts all of them side by side against the same design questions, so the trade-offs from every earlier topic become a single decision framework instead of five separate stories. "You're designing a matching engine — which concurrency model, and why not the others?" is the shape of question this topic exists to answer well.

Two questions, asked in this order, narrow the choice fast:

1. **Is the workload I/O-bound or CPU-bound?** I/O-bound (waiting on network, disk, timers) benefits from *concurrency* without needing *parallelism* — async/await's single-thread model fits well. CPU-bound (real computation) needs actual parallelism — multiple cores genuinely busy — which rules out a single-threaded event loop as the primary mechanism.
2. **Does the domain need shared mutable state, or does it decompose into independent units?** If state is inherently shared and contended (a single counter, a shared cache), threads-plus-primitives or lock-free structures fit. If the domain has natural, independent entities (per-user sessions, per-room state) or a pipeline shape (staged data transformation), actors or CSP remove the sharing problem structurally instead of managing it.

Every topic in this group maps onto one branch of these two questions — this framework is just naming the branches explicitly.

| | Threads | Async/await | Actors | CSP |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Memory model | Shared, mutable | Shared, but only one task runs at a time | Isolated — no shared state between actors | Isolated — communication only via channels |
| Failure isolation | None built-in — one thread's crash can corrupt shared state others read | Weak — an uncaught error can still affect shared state your code touches | Strong — supervision trees restart failed actors independently | Weak — no built-in supervision, a goroutine leak has no automatic recovery |
| Typical use case | CPU-bound parallelism, low-level primitives | I/O-bound servers, UI event handling | Independent stateful entities (sessions, devices, game rooms) | Data pipelines, worker fan-out/fan-in |
| Raw performance ceiling | Highest — direct memory access | High for I/O-bound work specifically | Lower — message serialization overhead | Lower — channel overhead, though typically less than actors' |

This table is the condensed form of every earlier topic's own compare section — the goal here is holding all four in view at once, not re-deriving each row from scratch.

slides.sectionTitle: Why "no shared state" sidesteps entire bug classes
slides.markdown:
It's worth stating precisely, one more time, because it's the single idea worth remembering from this entire group: actors and CSP don't make data races *less likely* through good practice — they make the specific bug class **unrepresentable**, the same way a strongly-typed language makes a whole category of type errors unrepresentable rather than merely rare.

Threads-plus-locks reduce race likelihood through discipline that has to hold on every code path, forever, including ones written by someone new to the codebase two years from now. Actors and CSP remove the capability to write the buggy code at all — there's no syntax for one actor to reach into another's private field, no way to "forget" a lock because there's no lock protecting a variable you could accidentally skip. This is a categorically stronger guarantee, not just a smaller probability.

None of this is free, and the fee is worth naming explicitly rather than treated as a footnote. Actors and CSP both pay real **message-passing overhead** — serialization or copying of data crossing between isolated units — that raw shared-memory threads simply don't pay, because reading a shared variable directly has essentially no marginal cost beyond the memory access itself.

For a workload with genuinely intense, fine-grained data sharing (a tight numeric kernel touching the same array from multiple threads thousands of times per millisecond), forcing that through message passing would be a severe performance regression relative to direct shared access — this is exactly why lock-free/STM (`lock-free-programming-and-stm`) exist as a third path: keep the direct-access performance, change the coordination mechanism instead of removing sharing altogether.

slides.sectionTitle: How production systems actually mix models
slides.markdown:
Real systems rarely commit to exactly one model end to end — they compose them at different layers, matching each layer's actual need:

- **An actor system built on top of a thread pool.** Akka doesn't give every actor its own OS thread — a pool of OS threads underneath executes actor message-processing, with the actor abstraction providing the isolation guarantee while the thread pool provides the actual parallel execution capacity. The actor model is the *programming model*; threads are the *execution substrate*.
- **An async/await server offloading CPU-bound work to a thread/process pool.** The event loop handles I/O-bound connection management; genuinely CPU-heavy per-request work gets dispatched to a separate pool so it doesn't stall the loop — exactly the fix `async-await-and-cooperative-concurrency`'s blocking-call pitfall called for.
- **A CSP worker pool using channels for coordination but lock-free structures for a shared metrics counter.** Not everything needs full actor/channel isolation — a simple shared counter is a legitimate case for `lock-free-programming-and-stm`'s narrow sweet spot, layered inside an otherwise CSP-shaped system.

The senior-level takeaway: "which model" is often the wrong question for a whole system — the right question is which model fits *each layer* of it.

slides.sectionTitle: Structured concurrency applies to all of them
slides.markdown:
`structured-concurrency`'s lifetime discipline isn't a sixth model competing with the others — it's a layer that applies on top of whichever model you picked. A structured scope can own child threads, child async coroutines, or (with more friction, since neither model has this discipline built in the same way) actors and CSP goroutines.

This is worth stating explicitly in an interview: naming a concurrency model for a design answers "how does work happen concurrently," while naming structured concurrency on top of it answers a separate, equally important question — "how do I guarantee that work doesn't outlive its purpose." A complete system design answer often needs both, and conflating them (treating structured concurrency as just another item in the same list as threads/actors/CSP) is a common, avoidable miss.

slides.sectionTitle: Picking wrong is a real, common interview miss
slides.markdown:
The most common failure mode in a "design the concurrency for X" interview answer isn't picking a bad model in isolation — it's picking a *popular* model reflexively without connecting it to the workload's actual shape. Reaching for actors because they sound sophisticated, for a problem that's really just "process this queue with a worker pool" (a CSP-shaped problem, or even just plain threads with a queue), is a real, common miss that reads as pattern-matching rather than reasoning.

The fix is procedural: name the workload's I/O-vs-CPU and shared-state-vs-independent-units shape *before* naming a model, out loud, in the interview. "This is I/O-bound with independent per-connection state, so I'd reach for async/await plus one lightweight task per connection" is a complete, defensible answer in one sentence — and it's the sentence a candidate who jumped straight to naming a favorite model never gets to say, because they never established why it fits.

"You're designing a matching engine — which concurrency model, and why not the others?" is a complete synthesis question, and a strong answer runs through the framework explicitly:

1. **Workload shape:** matching orders against a shared order book is CPU-bound, latency-critical, and centers on one piece of intensely shared, frequently-mutated state (the book itself) — not an I/O-bound or naturally-partitioned problem.
2. **Rule out async/await** — no I/O-bound waiting to overlap; the bottleneck is computation on shared state, which a single-threaded event loop wouldn't parallelize anyway.
3. **Rule out (or narrow) actors/CSP** — message-passing overhead on every single order touching the shared book would be a severe latency tax for a system where microseconds matter; isolation doesn't buy much when the whole point is one shared, contended resource.
4. **Land on a single-writer thread (or a carefully lock-free structure) owning the order book**, with other components (order intake, market data distribution) potentially using different models — an async I/O layer for network intake feeding a single dedicated matching thread, for instance.

Naming *why the other models don't fit*, not just why one does, is what separates a senior answer from a name-drop.

slides.sectionTitle: The whole group, in one sentence
slides.markdown:
Every model in this group is a different answer to the same question `threads-and-the-shared-memory-model` opened with — what do you do about concurrent access to state — and none of them is a universal winner: threads give you raw performance and raw risk, async/await gives you cheap concurrency for waiting-heavy work, actors and CSP remove sharing at the cost of message-passing overhead, lock-free/STM keep sharing but change the coordination primitive, and structured concurrency disciplines task lifetime on top of any of the above.

The skill this whole group is actually testing for isn't "which model do you know" — it's whether you can name a workload's real shape and pick (or compose) the model that shape actually calls for.
